Treasure of the Kingdom
TREZH-ur uhv thuh KING-duhm
noun phrase (kingdom parable)
From treasure, Latin thesaurus, a store of valuables; here the surpassing worth of the kingdom of heaven, laid up where moth and rust do not corrupt.

📖 Biblical Definition

The treasure of the kingdom is the surpassing, all-exceeding worth of the kingdom of heaven and of Christ its King, a worth so great that the man who finds it gladly parts with all he has to possess it. Our Lord commands, "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matt 6:19-20), and adds the searching word, "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Matt 6:21). He likens the kingdom to "treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field" (Matt 13:44), and again to "a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it" (Matt 13:45-46). The note in both parables is joy, not grudging sacrifice; the man counts all loss for the excellency of what he has found. This dictionary confesses that Christ and His kingdom are the pearl of great price, worth the forsaking of every earthly thing, and that the heart truly converted treasures Him above all and lays up its riches in heaven.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The treasure of the kingdom is the surpassing worth of Christ and His reign, laid up in heaven where it cannot perish. The parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl of great price teach that it is worth selling all to gain. The note is joy, not grudging sacrifice.

TREASURE OF THE KINGDOM, noun phrase. The surpassing worth of the kingdom of heaven and of Christ its King.

It is treasure laid up in heaven, where moth and rust do not corrupt nor thieves break through.

"Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field" (Matt 13:44).

It requires that a man count all things loss to gain it, and lay up his riches above; it forbids the hoarding of perishable wealth.

Its possession is joy, for the man sells all he has and buys the field with gladness.

📖 Key Scripture

Matt 6:19 — "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:"

Matt 6:21 — "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Matt 13:44 — "Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field."

Matt 13:46 — "Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The age inverts the parable, treating earthly wealth as the true treasure and the kingdom as one optional good among many, rather than the pearl worth selling all to gain.

expand to see more

The prosperity gospel turns the treasure of the kingdom upside down, making earthly riches the proof of God's favor and the kingdom a means to worldly gain, when Christ commands the opposite, to lay up treasure in heaven and count earthly wealth as that which moth and rust corrupt. The wider materialism of the age simply forgets the kingdom altogether and lays up its all on earth, so that where its treasure is, there its heart is also, far from God.

Recover the joy of the parables. The man who finds the hidden treasure and the merchant who finds the pearl do not part with their goods in grudging duty but for joy, counting the kingdom worth infinitely more than all they forsake. So the converted heart treasures Christ above every earthly thing and lays up its riches where they can never perish.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Treasure comes from Greek thesauros, a store or storehouse, used by Christ for the imperishable riches of the kingdom.

expand to see more

Greek thesauros, a store of valuables, lies behind both the "treasure" of Matt 6 and Matt 13.

The phrase "pearl of great price" renders margarites polutimos, a pearl of surpassing worth.

The verb "selleth all" (polei panta) marks the total cost gladly paid for the kingdom.

Latin thesaurus and Old French tresor give the English treasure.

Matt 6:21 ties the location of one's treasure to the disposition of one's heart.

Usage

"He preached that Christ is the pearl of great price, the treasure of the kingdom worth selling all to gain."

"She laid up her treasure in heaven, holding her earthly goods with a loose and grateful hand."

"The prosperity teacher reversed the parable, making earthly wealth the treasure and the kingdom a means to it."
